name: Impostor syndrome
statement: High achievers who cannot internalise their success believe they have fooled everyone, and expect to be found out as frauds.
meaning: The claim is about a gap between the record and the self-image. Someone holds degrees, promotions and praise, and reads every one of them as luck, charm, timing or an administrative error. Clance and Imes described four behaviours that maintain the belief once it is in place: diligence and hard work, intellectual flattery, using charm to win over a mentor whose approval is then discounted, and holding on to the impostor position to avoid what they took to be the social penalties on a confident woman. A woman may show one or more of them, they write, but seldom all. The belief is self-sealing, because each new success is explained away by the same machinery that explained the last one. What the term does not describe is a disorder. Bravata and colleagues state that impostor syndrome is not featured in the American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual and is not listed as a diagnosis in ICD-10, and they recommend that it be considered for inclusion in the DSM.

origin.who: Pauline Rose Clance and Suzanne Imes
origin.note: The paper is a clinical report, not an experiment. It describes five years of psychotherapy, interaction groups and college classes with over 150 high-achieving women, and contains no measurement, no comparison group and no statistics. The word 'syndrome' is not in it; the authors wrote 'impostor phenomenon'.

evidence: Clance and Imes list the groups their observations came from: 95 undergraduates and 10 doctoral faculty women at a private Midwestern college, 15 undergraduates, 20 graduate students and 10 faculty at a large southern university, six medical students, and 22 professional women in law, nursing, social work and other fields. Those numbers sum to 178, against the 'over 150' in the text. About a third were therapy clients; the rest were in groups or classes taught by the authors. All were women, mostly white and middle to upper class, aged 20 to 45. A footnote reports the authors' clinical impression that the phenomenon is rarer and milder in men, and calls for research. Measurement arrived later. Clance published the 20-item Clance Impostor Phenomenon Scale in 1985. Chrisman and colleagues compared it with the Perceived Fraudulence Scale in 1995, found three components they named Fake, Discount and Luck, and reported that impostor feelings were related to but substantially discriminable from depression, self-esteem, social anxiety and self-monitoring. Mak, Kleitman and Abbott appraised four impostor scales in 2019 and found the position weaker than its use suggests. The Clance scale and the others rest on multidimensional definitions yet report a single total and define no subscale scores, which their review calls a contradiction of the construct they are built on. It would be premature, they conclude, to classify the Clance scale as the gold standard measure.

replication.headline: The correlates reproduce across large samples, and the prevalence claim does not: the figure everyone quotes traces to a newspaper feature, while the largest review puts prevalence anywhere between 9% and 82% depending on the cutoff.
replication.detail: Bravata and colleagues searched Medline, Embase and PsycINFO from 1966 to May 2018 and found 66 articles describing 62 studies of 14,161 participants, 60% of them women. Prevalence ran 'from 9 to 82% largely depending on the screening tool and cutoff used'. Their sharpest illustration is a single sample: Chae and colleagues' 654 Korean Catholics gave 39% at a scale cutoff of 58 and 24% at a cutoff of 62. None of the 62 studies evaluated a treatment. Omar and colleagues later pooled 34 studies of 9,550 medical students and report prevalence of 49%, 95% CI 43% to 54%, with heterogeneity of I-squared 95.6%; their abstract concludes that the variance across measurement tools 'suggests that researchers may not be consistently measuring the same construct'. The associations hold up better than the counts. Rohrmann, Bechtoldt and Leonhardt tested 242 managers. The model that kept impostor feelings as a separate factor fitted better than models merging it with neuroticism, depression, apprehension, core self-evaluations or concern over mistakes. Their correlations were .48 for neuroticism, .48 for apprehension and -.46 for core self-evaluations. Fleischhauer and colleagues, in 209 adults, report r = -0.71 with self-esteem and r = 0.62 with neuroticism. Breit and colleagues' meta-analysis of 26 records and 91 effect sizes separates the two halves of perfectionism. The mean reliability-adjusted correlation was z = .747, 95% CI .632 to .863, for perfectionistic concerns, against z = .159, 95% CI .051 to .268, for perfectionistic strivings. Strivings showed no unique relationship once concerns were partialled out. The 70% claim has a shorter trail. Sakulku and Alexander's review writes that 'it is estimated that 70% of people will experience at least one episode of this Impostor Phenomenon in their lives', citing Gravois (2007), a Chronicle of Higher Education feature. ERIC's record of that feature summarises it as reporting research from the mid-1980s that about 70 percent of people have felt fraudulent. The published Clance work from that period is Matthews and Clance (1985), a description of 41 private-practice clients; Bravata's table of that study records its prevalence as not stated. No peer-reviewed source located in this search reports 70% as a measured prevalence.

study.cite: Bravata, D. M., Watts, S. A., Keefer, A. L., Madhusudhan, D. K., Taylor, K. T., Clark, D. M., Nelson, R. S., Cokley, K. O., & Hagg, H. K. (2020). Prevalence, predictors, and treatment of impostor syndrome: A systematic review. Journal of General Internal Medicine, 35(4), 1252-1275.

limits: There is no original experiment to repeat, so 'replication' here means whether later measurement recovers what the 1978 paper described. It partly does. Several figures could not be obtained. The Gravois feature sits behind the Chronicle's paywall, so the 70% sentence in this entry is read from Sakulku and Alexander and from ERIC's record, not from the feature itself. Gullifor and colleagues' workplace review returned HTTP 403, so only its Crossref abstract was read. Omar and colleagues' medical-education meta-analysis is described from its Crossref abstract. Clance's 1985 book, which carries the scale and its cutoffs, was not read. Chrisman and colleagues' sample size is not in their abstract and their paper was not opened. The prevalence literature is also skewed young: Bravata reports a weighted mean age of 20 years, with 34 of the 62 studies drawn from students. Searches covered Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, PMC, Frontiers, ERIC, Springer, Wiley and general web search.
misreadings: The 70% figure is the main one, and it is quoted as though a survey produced it. The second is the word 'syndrome', which Clance and Imes did not use and which implies a clinical category that neither the DSM nor ICD-10 contains. Feenstra and colleagues argue for keeping 'phenomenon' on the ground that 'syndrome' implies a medical model of dysfunction inside the individual, and that the environment does part of the work. A third misreading treats a questionnaire score above some cutoff as a diagnosis, when the same 654 people can be 39% impostors or 24% impostors depending on which cutoff is chosen. The last is that it is a women's condition. That is what the 1978 sample was, by construction, and Bravata found impostor syndrome common among men and women alike, from adolescents to late-stage professionals.
